---
title: "Agentic coding: build a clinical tool in an hour, then find what is wrong with it"
subtitle: "AIM-5 · AIM-2 · AIM-4 · about 75 minutes"
---

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

1. Say what a coding agent does that a chatbot does not, and why that changes
   who is responsible for checking the result.
2. Build a working single-page clinical calculator from a plain-language
   prompt, in a browser, with no install.
3. Verify the generated clinical logic against the original publication or
   MDCalc, and find at least one discrepancy or edge-case failure in the tool
   you just built.
4. Explain why that tool is not a medical device, and name what would have to
   change for it to become one.
5. State the rule about patient information in consumer and institutional AI
   tools, and say why it is not a formality.
:::

**Time.** About 20 minutes of reading, 15 minutes of watching, 35 minutes of
building and checking, and 5 minutes for the Check. You need your institutional
ChatGPT Edu account (its *canvas* pane previews the page you build) and one
MDCalc tab. Nothing installs. Alternatives, and what each one asks of you at
signup, are in the Do block.

## The spreadsheet on the shared drive

Fourth month of intern year, hepatology service. The second-year resident on
your team built a web page over a weekend. You paste in five lab values and it
gives you a MELD-Na score, the number that ranks patients for a liver
transplant, and tells you whether the patient is above the listing threshold.
It is bookmarked on every workroom computer. The attending mentioned it on
rounds as an example of initiative. Everyone uses it, and you have used it
twice today.

This morning the transplant coordinator calls about a patient with a
creatinine of 1.6 who has been on dialysis since Tuesday. The team's number
for her is 24. The coordinator's number is 32. Eight points is the difference
between waiting and being listed. The coordinator wants to know where 24 came
from.

::: {.app-mock}
<div class="bar">⬤ ⬤ ⬤ &nbsp; teamtools.local/meld &nbsp;·&nbsp; MELD-Na quick calc</div>
<div class="body">
<h4>MELD-Na</h4>
<div class="row"><span>Bilirubin (mg/dL)</span><span>3.4</span></div>
<div class="row"><span>INR</span><span>1.9</span></div>
<div class="row flag"><span>Creatinine (mg/dL)</span><span>1.6</span></div>
<div class="row"><span>Sodium (mmol/L)</span><span>134</span></div>
<div class="row flag"><span>Dialysis ≥2× this week</span><span>(no field)</span></div>
<div class="score"><b>24</b><span>MELD-Na · below listing threshold</span></div>
</div>
<div class="banner">Built with ChatGPT · for team use</div>
<div class="fine">Illustrative tool for this chapter, drawn in CSS; not a real product. The highlighted rows are where the two numbers part company.</div>
:::

Look at the tool before reading on. It has no place to say the patient is on
dialysis. That is not a bug in the arithmetic. The formula the resident asked
for was implemented exactly as described. What the description left out was a
rule the original paper attached to the formula: when a patient has had
dialysis twice in the past week, creatinine is set to 4.0 before it enters the
equation, whatever the lab says. Apply that rule to this patient and the score
moves from 24 to 32. The coordinator is right. (The tool also accepts a sodium
of 118 without comment, though the paper bounds sodium at 125; that rule did
not matter for this patient. It will for the next one.)

Nobody lied, nobody was careless in the ordinary sense, and the tool worked
perfectly for the first thirty patients, none of whom were on dialysis. The
resident asked a language model for a MELD-Na calculator and got one. What
the resident did not do was ask what the paper says happens at the edges,
and nobody on the team, including you, checked. The patient, who would have
waited unlisted on the strength of a number from a weekend project, does not
know the project exists.

This chapter is about building a tool like that yourself, in about fifteen
minutes, and then spending twenty finding what is wrong with it. The build is
the easy part now. The checking is the skill.

## Why this matters

You will meet a tool like the resident's within the year, because they are
cheap to make and every team has someone who makes them. Some are
spreadsheets. Some are web pages. Increasingly they are built by describing
what you want to a model and accepting what comes back. The person who built
it is usually proud of it, the attending is usually pleased, and nobody has
been asked to check it, because checking a colleague's tool is not a job
anyone is assigned.

Unchecked tools that a whole team relies on have a history that predates
language models. In October 2020, Public Health England's official figures
missed nearly 16,000 positive COVID-19 results over a week, and days later only
half of those patients had been contacted for tracing [@pmid:33023893]. The
reported cause, in the clippings below, was that results were being collected
in an Excel file format with a row limit, and rows past the limit were silently
dropped. The spreadsheet did not crash. It did what it was told.

::: {.press-clips}
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">BBC News · technology</div><a class="hl" href="https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-54423988">Excel: Why using Microsoft's tool caused Covid-19 results to be lost</a><div class="date">5 October 2020</div></div>
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">The Guardian · politics</div><a class="hl" href="https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2020/oct/05/how-excel-may-have-caused-loss-of-16000-covid-tests-in-england">Covid: how Excel may have caused loss of 16,000 test results in England</a><div class="date">5 October 2020</div></div>
<div class="press-clip"><div class="src">Slate · technology</div><a class="hl" href="https://slate.com/technology/2020/10/u-k-covid-19-spike-caused-by-microsoft-excel-error.html">An Outdated Version of Excel Led the U.K. to Undercount COVID-19 Cases</a><div class="date">7 October 2020</div></div>
:::

A quieter version runs through the research literature: roughly one in five
genomics papers with supplementary gene lists in Excel contained gene names
that the spreadsheet had silently converted to dates [@pmid:27552985]. The
tool was fine. The tool was not checked against what it was being used for.

In three months you will be the intern with the bookmark, or the intern who
built it. Either way the skill you need is the same: take a tool that seems to
work, decide what it would take to trust it, and go and look.

## The idea

### A chatbot answers; an agent acts

Everything you have used so far in this course is a chatbot: you type, it
writes, you copy what you want out of the reply. A **coding agent** is the same
kind of model wrapped in a loop. It plans a step, takes an action in the world
(writes a file, runs a program, reads the output), observes what happened, and
plans the next step. The actions are real: files change, code runs. Because
the actions are real, agents run with **permissions**, a list of what they are
allowed to touch. @fig-chatbot-agent shows the two shapes.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-chatbot-agent
%%| fig-cap: "Two ways to use the same model. A chatbot writes text and stops. A coding agent loops: plan, act on real files or programs, observe the result, and continue, inside a boundary of permissions you set."
flowchart LR
  subgraph C["Chatbot"]
    direction TB
    p1[Your prompt] --> t1[Model writes text]
    t1 --> u1[You copy what you want]
  end
  subgraph A["Coding agent"]
    direction TB
    p2[Your goal] --> plan[Plan a step]
    plan --> act[Act: write a file, run code]
    act --> obs[Observe the result]
    obs --> plan
    obs --> done[Show you what it built]
  end
```

The tools you will use today sit between the two. When your chatbot opens a
side panel, writes a web page into it, and shows you the running page, that is
the smallest possible version of the loop: the model wrote a file and the
browser ran it. You are the observer. The full-strength agents, the ones that
work inside a folder of files on your own computer, are mentioned at the end
of the chapter and are deliberately not used here; they need an install and a
terminal, and neither is the point.

The point is what changes when the output is something that *runs*. A wrong
sentence in a chatbot reply sits there until you read it. A wrong rule in a
calculator does its work silently, on every patient, until somebody compares
its answer to another source. The mechanism that produces the error is the one
from the critical appraisal chapter, a plausible continuation rather than a
lookup, but the error now has a place to hide.

### Two names for the same thing

In February 2025 Andrej Karpathy, one of the founders of OpenAI, coined "vibe
coding" for the practice of describing what you want, accepting what the model
produces, and never reading the code. Collins Dictionary named it word of the
year for 2025. A year later Karpathy declared it passé and proposed "agentic
engineering" instead: directing and reviewing an agent's work rather than
accepting it [VERIFY: Karpathy posts of 2 Feb 2025 and Feb 2026; Collins WOTY 2025; secondary sources in research notes]{.verify}.

Both terms will be gone before you finish residency. The shift between them is
the durable part. The first name treats judgment as something you set aside;
the second treats it as the scarce input. You are about to do the first for
fifteen minutes so that you can practise the second for twenty.

The right mental model for the model, borrowed from the author's talks on the
subject, is a capable but junior colleague: fast, fluent, willing, and in need
of clear instructions and review. You review its work the way a senior reviews
a junior's: not by trusting the confident tone, but by checking the parts that
would hurt someone if wrong.

### Three ways the tool you just built is wrong

A generated calculator can fail in three ways, and they fail independently.
Each has a matching check in the Do block.

| Failure | What it looks like | How you catch it |
|---|---|---|
| **The rule** | A point value, cutoff, or coefficient is wrong, or a rule from the original paper is missing (the dialysis rule; the sodium bounds; whether a score is only applied above a threshold) | Compare every rule to the original publication, not to your memory of it |
| **The edge** | The tool does something the builder never imagined for inputs the builder never tried: nothing checked, two mutually exclusive boxes checked, a value outside the range the score was derived on | Try the inputs the builder did not: empty, contradictory, extreme |
| **The version** | The score has more than one published form, and the tool does not say which one it implements (Wells' criteria exist in a three-tier and a two-tier form; the transplant system replaced MELD-Na with MELD 3.0 in 2023) | Ask which version, and check that against what your team, and MDCalc, actually use |

: Three independent failures. A tool can pass two and fail the third. {#tbl-three-failures}

The first row is where models are weakest and where the evidence is clearest.
When ChatGPT was asked to perform 48 kinds of medical calculation directly, it
got one trial in three wrong; giving the model a purpose-built calculation
tool to call instead of doing the arithmetic itself cut the error rate
thirteenfold, from 64% to 4.8% [@pmid:40097720]. Read that finding carefully,
because it cuts both ways. A model *doing* clinical arithmetic in its head is
unreliable. A model *writing code* that does the arithmetic is much better,
which is exactly why the tool you build today will mostly work. But the code
only encodes the rules the model put in it, and the rules it leaves out leave
no trace.

The second row is where non-programmers are weakest. When medical students
spent three hours building health apps by prompting, every group produced a
working prototype, and no group implemented any protection for the data the
app collected; the authors' summary was that lowering the barrier to building
is not the same as lowering the barrier to building safely [@pmid:42394077].
An editorial in the laboratory medicine literature gives the pattern a name
you will recognise from the wards, the illusion of competence: syntactically
correct code that looks professional is most convincing to the people least
equipped to find its flaws, and there is a real difference between code that
runs and code that is safe to run on patients [@pmid:42695169].

The third row is the quiet one. A nursing research group used a coding agent
to run a logistic regression and checked every output against a published
reference: the coefficients and *p* values matched, and an error in one
confidence interval was missed on first review and caught only on a second
pass [@pmid:42611917]. The tool was mostly right, which is the condition
under which people stop checking.

### What "checked" looks like

The counterexample is worth knowing because it shows the bar is reachable. A
cardiology group built a web calculator for three acute coronary syndrome risk
scores with ChatGPT writing the code, then compared its output against 226
registry patients whose scores had been computed independently. Agreement was
exact (*r* = 1.000 for both scores with a registry comparator), and the paper
says so in the methods, with the registry named [@pmid:40462782]. That is not
a large study and it is not clinical validation, which the authors are careful
to say. It is what a *technical* check looks like: an external source of truth,
a fixed set of cases, and a written result.

The resident's tool in the workroom had none of those. Yours, in thirty
minutes, will have a small version of all three.

### The named hazard

A 2026 framework for governing clinician-built software, VIBE-HI, puts one
hazard at the centre and gives it a name: **comprehension abdication**, the
surrender of understanding to the system that generated the code. If you
cannot say in plain language what your tool does for every input, you cannot
anticipate how it fails, and you cannot safely change it [@pmid:42564266]. The
framework sorts tools into four risk tiers by four questions, redrawn in
@tbl-tiers from the paper's description.

| The question | Pushes the tier up when |
|---|---|
| Does it touch identifiable patient data? | Real names, medical record numbers, or anything that could be re-identified |
| How close is it to a clinical decision? | Its output changes what is done to a patient, rather than what a student studies |
| Who uses it, and how much do they understand it? | People other than the builder, who did not see it made |
| How many patients does it reach? | A team, a service, a hospital |

: The four criteria VIBE-HI uses to place a tool on its green-to-red scale, in plain words. The tier is set by the worst answer, not the average. The tiers themselves map to regulatory obligations the ethics and regulation chapter covers. {#tbl-tiers}

Run the resident's tool through the four questions. It handles pasted labs
(the first question depends on what people paste, which nobody controls); its
output is a listing decision; it is used by a whole team, most of whom never
saw it built; it reaches every patient on the service. A study aid for one
person answers all four questions the other way. The tool did not change
between those two descriptions. Its use did.

![Which is why, for anything that matters, the last panel is the correct
answer more often than engineers like. xkcd 2030, *Voting Software*, by
Randall Munroe, [CC BY-NC 2.5](https://xkcd.com/license.html); the
non-commercial condition travels with the image if you reuse this
chapter.](../images/voting_software.png){#fig-xkcd-voting .comic fig-alt="xkcd comic in three panels. In the first two, an aircraft engineer and an elevator engineer are asked whether their systems are safe and say yes, with caveats. In the third, a software engineer asked about voting software says nobody should use it for anything important, and the questioner asks whether they should just use paper."}

### Where a toy becomes a device

Whether software counts as a medical device in the United States turns, for
tools like this one, on the FDA's criteria for *non-device clinical decision
support*. The criterion that matters for a calculator is whether the clinician
can independently review the basis for the recommendation: a tool that shows
the score, the inputs, the rule it applied, and where the rule came from is
one a clinician can check; a bare number is not. A personal study aid that a
student uses to practise scores is not a device. The same page, bookmarked on
the workroom computers and used to decide who gets listed, is a different
question, and the answer depends on what it shows and who relies on it. The
FDA revised its decision-support guidance in January 2026; what the revision
changed, and the rest of the regulatory picture, belong to the ethics and
regulation chapter [VERIFY: FDA CDS guidance, revised 6 January 2026, current text]{.verify}.

For this chapter, the working rule is simpler than the regulation. **Toy, not
device.** Your tool carries a banner saying so, in the prompt, before it
exists. That is not classroom theatre. It is the professional habit of
labelling AI-assisted work, rehearsed on something harmless.

::: {.callout-note title="Who signs"}
When the team's number is wrong, the person accountable is the clinician who
acted on it, not the resident who built the page. Regulation may eventually
reach the builder; the chart reaches you first. The practical consequence for
a note: record the score and the source you took it from, and make the source
one that has been checked by someone other than a colleague, which today means
the original publication or an established calculator such as MDCalc. If a
team tool has been validated locally, your institution's policy will say so,
and the ethics and regulation chapter takes up what to document when it has.
:::

### Patient information, once more

Your institutional ChatGPT Edu account is not covered by a business associate
agreement for clinical use unless your institution says it is. A business
associate agreement is the contract that makes a vendor legally responsible
for protecting patient data; without one, pasting a real patient's labs into
the tool is a privacy violation regardless of intent. Consumer and free tiers
never have one, and free tiers may use what you type to train the next model.

The rule for today, and for every tool you build until someone with authority
tells you otherwise: **every number you type is one you invented.** Not a
de-identified real patient, not a classmate, not yourself. Invented. The
pattern you are rehearsing, a chat window with a patient's labs in it, is
exactly how patient data leaks when the same window is reused for real work.

::: {.callout-important title="Nothing worth stealing"}
Around 40% of programs generated by an early coding assistant in
security-relevant scenarios contained a vulnerability [@doi:10.1109/SP46214.2022.9833571],
and in a controlled study, people with an AI assistant wrote less secure code
and were more confident that it was secure [@doi:10.1145/3576915.3623157].
Both studies predate current models and the numbers will have moved. The
direction is what matters: you are not going to security-review a page you
built in fifteen minutes. So the rule is not "make it secure"; it is *put
nothing in it worth stealing.* No credentials, no identifiers, no real data.
:::

## Watch or listen

**Video.** Andrej Karpathy, *Software Is Changing (Again)*, keynote at Y
Combinator's AI Startup School, San Francisco, 17 June 2025 (published 19 June
2025; 39 min). <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ>. Also on the Y
Combinator podcast feed if you prefer audio; YouTube's captions are automatic
and adequate.

Fifteen minutes is enough. Skip the opening on "Software 3.0" if you are short
of time and go to the middle third, where he describes *partial autonomy*
apps and the *autonomy slider*: the idea that the useful question about an AI
tool is not whether it is autonomous but how much autonomy you have handed it
for this task, and how fast you can check what it did. Listen for the phrase
about keeping the AI "on a leash." Then ask, for the tool you are about to
build, where the slider is set and who is holding the leash. The person who
coined "vibe coding" is also the person telling you to verify.

**Instead, or as well.** The author's own decks: [From Chatbots to Coding
Agents](https://talks.seandavis.net/2026-06-18-cshl/) (June 2026) walks the
plan-act-observe loop in @fig-chatbot-agent with live examples, and the
recording of the [October 2025 live vibe-coding
session](https://talks.seandavis.net/2025-10-17-idpt-vibe-coding/) from this
course's predecessor shows a calculator being built in front of a class, with
the mistakes left in.

## Do

::: {.callout-warning title="Invented numbers only"}
Every value you type into the tool today is one you made up. No patient from a
rotation, however de-identified you think it is; no classmate; no family
member. Consumer tools carry no business associate agreement, and your
institutional account is not cleared for patient data unless your institution
has told you so in writing. If a test case needs a sodium of 118, invent a
patient with a sodium of 118.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Which tool, and what it asks of you"}
**ChatGPT Edu (your institutional account).** Ask for the page and it should
open in the *canvas* pane with a preview button that runs it. This is the
assumed path. If canvas does not appear, your workspace administrator may
have turned off canvas code execution; use the fallback below.
[VERIFY: canvas preview enabled in the institutional ChatGPT Edu workspace]{.verify}

**Fallback that works with any chatbot, including Copilot.** Ask for "a single
HTML file". Copy the whole code block into a plain text editor (Notepad,
TextEdit in plain-text mode), save it as `calc.html`, and double-click it. Your
browser opens it. Nothing is installed; you have made a file, which is what
the agent would have done for you.

**Claude.ai** free tier builds and hosts the page as an *artifact* with a
shareable link, which is convenient for the live session. Signup requires a
phone number. If you would rather not give one, you lose nothing by using the
paths above. **Google AI Studio** needs a Google account and no phone; it is
the second alternative.

Free tiers may use your prompts for training. That is fine for invented
numbers and a prompt about a public scoring system. It would not be fine for
anything else.
:::

### Part A: build it (12 minutes)

**Step 1. Pick a score.** Choose the one closest to your specialty from
@tbl-menu. Each has a single original publication you will check against, and
each has at least one edge the model tends to miss. If none fits, use
CHA₂DS₂-VASc; it is the one the specimen below is written for.

| Specialty | Score | Original publication | Where the edges are |
|---|---|---|---|
| Medicine, cardiology, neurology | CHA₂DS₂-VASc (stroke risk in atrial fibrillation) | Lip et al., *Chest* 2010 [@pmid:19762550] | Two age bands that must be mutually exclusive; the "female sex" point, which some current guidelines no longer score; the annual stroke-risk percentages come from a *different* paper [@pmid:22246443] |
| Emergency medicine | Wells' criteria for pulmonary embolism | Wells et al., *Thromb Haemost* 2000 [@pmid:10744147] | Half-point items and rounding; a three-tier and a two-tier version with different cutoffs; "PE is the most likely diagnosis" is a judgment, not a finding |
| Surgery, gastroenterology, transplant | MELD-Na | Kim et al., *NEJM* 2008 [@pmid:18768945]; MELD itself, Kamath et al., *Hepatology* 2001 [@pmid:11172350] | Values below 1.0 are set to 1.0; creatinine capped at 4.0 and set to 4.0 with dialysis; sodium bounded 125–137; the sodium term applies only above a MELD threshold; MELD 3.0 replaced it for listing in 2023 |
| Critical care, emergency medicine | qSOFA | Seymour et al., *JAMA* 2016 [@pmid:26903335] | The Glasgow Coma Scale cutoff (any score below 15, not a lower threshold); the systolic pressure boundary is ≤100, not <100; what the score is *for* (screening outside the ICU, not diagnosis) |
| Psychiatry, primary care, pediatrics | PHQ-9 | Kroenke et al., *J Gen Intern Med* 2001 [@pmid:11556941] | Nine items scored 0–3 and the severity bands between them; item 9, on self-harm, needs a response the calculator should not leave to a colour |
| Radiology | Fleischner 2017 incidental pulmonary nodule follow-up | MacMahon et al., *Radiology* 2017 [@pmid:28240562] | A decision table, not a sum: solid versus subsolid, single versus multiple, size bands, and a risk category; the guideline explicitly excludes several populations, and the tool will not know that unless told |

: The menu. Every publication was checked in PubMed for this chapter; the edges column is where to look first in Part B. {#tbl-menu}

**Step 2. Paste the starter prompt**, with your score substituted, into a
fresh conversation. Use it verbatim the first time; the guardrails are inside
it on purpose, and so is the wording. What comes back depends on how the
request is phrased, and the same prompt produces different code on different
days. Using the fixed text means your result reflects the model, not your
fluency in its dialect; if English is not your first language, that is the
point.

> Build a single-page web app, as one self-contained HTML file, that
> calculates the `<score>`. Show each input as a checkbox or numeric field
> with its point value or coefficient visible. Display the running total and
> the interpretation the original publication attaches to it. Add a prominent
> red banner: "Educational prototype only — not validated for clinical
> decision-making." In a footnote, cite the original publication for the
> score and say exactly which version of the score you implemented, so I can
> independently verify every rule against MDCalc and the paper before I trust
> the output.

**Step 3. Iterate twice.** Whatever comes back, ask for two changes, one at a
time, and watch what the model does to the rest of the page each time:

- "Colour the interpretation by risk tier."
- "Add a 'clear all' button, and tell me what the score shows when nothing is
  entered."

The second request is a check disguised as a feature. Read the answer.

You now have a working tool, it took about ten minutes, and it probably looks
better than the resident's. Do not share it yet.

### Part B: break it (15 minutes)

Open MDCalc and the original paper from @tbl-menu side by side with your tool.
Run three invented cases through all three sources and record the results in
the template below.

**Case 1, ordinary.** A patient squarely inside the score's intended
population, with nothing unusual. All three should agree. If they do not, you
have found a rule error and can stop here, because you have already met the
objective; note it and continue anyway.

**Case 2, the edge.** Take the edges column for your score and build a patient
who lives on one of them: a dialysis patient for MELD-Na, a sodium of 118, a
Glasgow score of 14 for qSOFA, a 6 mm subsolid nodule in a patient under 35 for
Fleischner, a 74-year-old and a 75-year-old for CHA₂DS₂-VASc. Compare the
three sources.

**Case 3, the nonsense.** Give the tool something no patient has. Both age
bands ticked. A negative creatinine. Every box checked and then every box
unchecked. A blank form. The question is not whether the tool refuses (it
usually will not) but whether you can say, before pressing anything, what it
will do, and whether what it does is safe or silent.

::: {.callout-tip title="Specimen: what to expect, and what to look for" collapse="true"}
**Expected behaviour, not a recorded run.** The two specimens below are
constructed from the failure patterns in @tbl-menu and the published
evidence above; a live run of the starter prompt was attempted for this
chapter and did not complete in time to be recorded, so nothing here is
presented as what a particular model produced on a particular day. Run the
prompt yourself and compare.

**CHA₂DS₂-VASc, expected.** The page will almost certainly get the eight
point values right and sum them correctly; that is the easy part, and the
one-in-three arithmetic failure above is about the model doing sums in prose,
not code. Look instead at three places. First, the two age boxes: if both
"65–74" and "≥75" can be ticked at once, the page can produce a score of 3
for age, which no patient has. Second, the stroke-risk percentages beside
each score: the page will print a column of numbers with a footnote naming
Lip et al. 2010, but the numbers most tools print come from a different
cohort [@pmid:22246443], and the two tables disagree; if the footnote does
not say which, that is the version failure. Third, the "female sex" box:
scored 1 in the 2010 paper, treated differently by newer guidelines; a page
that scores it without saying which guideline it follows has chosen for you.

**MELD-Na, expected.** The formula will be right. What tends to be missing
is exactly what the opening scenario turned on: no dialysis field, so
creatinine is never set to 4.0; no floor at 1.0 for values below it; no
bounds on sodium, so a sodium of 118 enters the equation raw; and no check
that the sodium term applies only above the MELD threshold. Ask the page for
a patient on dialysis and one with a sodium of 118, then compare to MDCalc.

Your run will differ from these expectations in both directions. Models
change monthly and the same prompt produces different code on different
days. The pattern is what to look for: the arithmetic is usually right; the
rules at the edges are where to read.
:::

**Record it.** Copy this into a document; it is your artifact for the live
session.

```
Tool used: ___________________   Model version if shown: ____________
Score built: __________________  Version the tool says it implements: ________

Case            Inputs (invented)         My tool   MDCalc   Paper    Agree?
1 ordinary      _______________________   _____     _____    _____    Y / N
2 edge          _______________________   _____     _____    _____    Y / N
3 nonsense      _______________________   _____     _____    _____    Y / N

Discrepancy or edge failure found (at least one; "none" needs a reason):
________________________________________________________________________
Which of the three failures in the table is it: rule / edge / version?
________________________________________________________________________
The one change I would make before letting anyone else use it:
________________________________________________________________________
```

"None found" is an acceptable answer only with a sentence saying which edges
you tried. A tool that survived three cases is not validated; it is three
cases old.

### Part C: explain it, then place it (8 minutes)

**The comprehension test.** In four sentences, without opening the code, write
what your tool does for: an ordinary patient, the edge case, the nonsense
case, and a blank form. If you cannot write the fourth sentence, ask the model
"what does the page show when nothing is entered, and why?", read the answer
against the page, and then write it. This is the test the resident never took.

**The device paragraph.** One paragraph answering three questions. Is your
tool, as it is, a medical device? (No; say why, using the phrase "study aid"
and the word "banner".) What would have to change for that answer to change?
(Name at least two of the four questions in @tbl-tiers.) And if your tool
showed only a bare score, with no inputs, rule, or citation visible, which
non-device criterion would it fail?

**The one sentence.** Write the sentence you would say to a co-intern who
shows you a calculator they built last night. It should contain a verb that
means *compare against something outside the tool*.

## Check

Score yourself against this before moving on.

| You have | Meets | Falls short |
|---|---|---|
| The chatbot-versus-agent distinction (objective 1) | You can say what the loop adds (acts on real files, observes, repeats, inside permissions) and why a running artifact hides errors a reply does not | "An agent is a smarter chatbot" |
| A working tool (objective 2) | Runs in a browser, shows inputs and total, carries the banner, cites the paper and names the version | Runs, but the banner or citation is missing, or the version is unstated |
| Three recorded cases (objective 3) | Each compared against MDCalc *and* the original paper; at least one discrepancy or edge failure named, and sorted as rule, edge, or version | "It matched MDCalc" with no edge case tried |
| The comprehension test (objective 3) | Four sentences, including the blank form, written before opening the code | The fourth sentence is missing or copied from the model |
| The device paragraph (objective 4) | Says why it is a study aid now, names two of the four questions that would change that, and names the criterion a bare score fails | "It's not a device because it's just a prototype" |
| The PHI rule (objective 5) | You can say what a business associate agreement is, that your institutional account does not have one for clinical use unless told, and why invented numbers are the rule | "Don't put patient data in ChatGPT" without the reason |
| The one sentence | Contains a verb meaning *compare against an outside source* | "Be careful with it" |

## The standing question

*What does this change about how you'll practice?* Write it down before you
close this chapter. Two specifics. First, go back to the workroom. The
coordinator is on the phone, the team's number is 24, hers is 32, and the
bookmark is on every computer. What do you say to her, what do you say to the
resident who built it, and what happens to the bookmark? Second, the next tool
you build yourself, or are handed by a colleague: name the three cases you
will run through it before it touches a decision, and the outside source each
one is compared against. One word is not an answer to either.

## Summary

- A chatbot writes; an agent acts, observes, and repeats inside permissions you
  set. The tools you used today are the smallest version of that loop, and
  the full ones need an install this chapter deliberately avoids.
- A running tool hides errors a reply does not. The arithmetic is usually
  right; the rules at the edges, and the version of the score, are where a
  generated calculator fails.
- A model doing clinical arithmetic in its head is wrong about a third of the
  time; a model writing code that does it is far better, and still only
  encodes the rules it was told about.
- Comprehension abdication is the named hazard: if you cannot say what your
  tool does for every input, you cannot say how it fails.
- Four questions move a tool from study aid toward device: patient data,
  closeness to a decision, who uses it, how many patients. The tool need not
  change for the answers to.
- Every number you type is one you invented; nothing worth stealing goes into
  a page you will not security-review; the banner goes in the prompt.
- The coordinator was right, and the team's spreadsheet was three cases old.

## Go deeper

**Papers**

- VIBE-HI, the governance framework behind @tbl-tiers, with its tiers mapped to
  regulation [@pmid:42564266]; and the laboratory-medicine editorial on the
  illusion of competence [@pmid:42695169].
- The clinical-calculation study behind the one-in-three figure
  [@pmid:40097720], and the cardiology group's technical validation of a
  ChatGPT-built calculator against a registry [@pmid:40462782], which is the
  model for what your Part B could become.
- Two views of the same practice from inside medicine: an editorial arguing
  it democratises biomedical software [@pmid:40598546], and a medical-education
  piece that built two teaching simulations this way [@pmid:40202513].
- The one evaluated medical-education app built by prompting, an ECG tutor
  compared against control sites, with mixed and inconsistent effects on exam
  performance [@doi:10.3390/ai7060223]. Building fast is not the same as
  building something that works.
- The security studies quoted above [@doi:10.1109/SP46214.2022.9833571;
  @doi:10.1145/3576915.3623157], for the numbers and their dates.

**Talks**

- [From Chatbots to Coding Agents](https://talks.seandavis.net/2026-06-18-cshl/)
  and [AI Agents for Biomedical Knowledge Work](https://talks.seandavis.net/2026-07-28-umihc/),
  the author's decks this chapter's framing comes from; the second has the
  privacy-and-trust section in full.

**If you want to go further**

- The full-strength agents, Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and GitHub Copilot
  in an editor, need a local install, a terminal, and in most cases a paid
  plan; the student Copilot plan paused new signups in April 2026
  [VERIFY: current status of the GitHub Copilot student plan]{.verify}. Try
  one after the course, on a project with nothing in it worth stealing.
- Google Colab runs Python notebooks in a browser with a Google account and no
  install, and its built-in agent can run a whole data-analysis workflow from
  a prompt. This course's predecessor used it for a public insurance-cost
  dataset. The completed notebook is a good appraisal object: ask what the
  agent decided without being asked, and what you would want to know before
  believing its R².
